---
title: "Review and continuous improvement"
description: "What happens to an analysis after it is released, and how the next piece of work gets better because of it."
---

*After release, once the analysis is in use. [Where this sits in the
lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

Assurance asks whether the analysis was done well. Review asks whether it did any good, and it asks
after release rather than before it. The two questions are different and this section answers the
second one.

::: {.callout-note title="This is not peer review" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Peer review and independent challenge happen **during** the work. They gate release, and they are in
[section 6, doing the work](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd), with the roles defined in
[section 3](../03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd).

The Review stage happens **after** delivery, and it repeats. It is evaluation rather than assurance,
and what it produces feeds the next piece of work rather than this one.

Both are called review in ordinary speech. If you are looking for how to get your work checked
before it goes out, section 6 is the page you want.
:::

## Why this stage exists

Analysis that is never looked at again cannot tell you whether it was worth producing. Four sources
ask for what this section describes:

| Source | What it asks for |
|---|---|
| **GovS 010 section 6.13** | Proposals are required to include proportionate provision for monitoring and evaluation before, during and after implementation |
| **GovS 010 section 6.10** | Lessons captured throughout the cycle, evaluated, and acted on. Senior officers update knowledge sources and communicate learning |
| **Code of Practice for Statistics 3.0, Standards 8, 9 and 10** | The Value pillar: relevance to users, clarity of presentation, accessibility of the output. All three are judged after release |
| **Magenta Book, chapter 6** | The use and dissemination of evaluation findings, including building an evaluation culture and being open about what was found |

The Value pillar is the one worth noticing. Standards 8, 9 and 10 bind official statistics and they
are judged on the released output, not the production process. This section is where NHSBSA meets
them.

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-review.qmd >}}

## What review covers

Seven activities. They are the ones NHSBSA already does, and they are here so that they are expected
rather than optional.

- **Decisions taken and policy changes informed.** What actually changed because of this analysis.
- **Usage.** Downloads, page views, requests, onward citation. Whatever the publication route
  records.
- **Ongoing usefulness.** User research with the people who use the output, asking whether it still
  answers their question.
- **Case studies.** How the data has been used, written down while someone still remembers.
- **Trend changes the analysis may have influenced.** Where the analysis was meant to move something,
  did it move.
- **Improvements to regular analysis.** What the last cycle showed could be better.
- **Decommissioning.** Analysis that is no longer useful should stop being produced. This is a
  finding, not a failure.

The first four are Code Standards 8, 9 and 10 in practice. The last three are GovS 010 section 6.13.

## When review happens, and who owns it

Review is not something to fit in when there is time. It has a trigger, an owner and a cadence, and
they scale with the assurance level set in
[section 5](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd).

| Assurance level | Trigger | Owner | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level 1 Standard | On request, or when the output changes | The analyst who produced it | At each reissue |
| Level 2 Enhanced | Scheduled | The commissioner, with the analyst | Annually, or at each reissue if more frequent |
| Level 3 Comprehensive, and Level 4 BCA | Scheduled, and on any material change | The commissioner, with the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer | Annually, and before any reuse for a new purpose |

**Why annual.** It is the longest interval at which an assumption can go stale without anyone
noticing, and anything shorter will not survive contact with workload. Business Critical work
reviews before reuse for a new purpose as well, because a new purpose is the change most likely to
invalidate the assumptions the original was built on. Level 1 needs no cadence at all: it is reviewed
when it is reissued.

::: {.callout-important title="The monthly cycle" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
NHSBSA runs a review cycle **monthly** for regular and ongoing outputs, checking that what has been
produced was peer reviewed, that it was completed correctly, and that it is still doing its job.

**No standard asks for that.** GovS 010 section 6.13 asks for proportionate provision and says
nothing about frequency. The Code's Value pillar is judged at release. The Magenta Book describes the
activity and not the cadence. The monthly cycle is a place where NHSBSA goes beyond what is required,
and it is written down here so that it survives a change of staff and so that it can be evidenced.

It covers regular published outputs. It looks at what changed and what went wrong rather than
reapproving what did not, and it is chaired by the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.
:::

## Lessons, and how they get back to the start

A lesson that stays in the review is not a lesson. GovS 010 section 6.10 asks for lessons to be
identified, evaluated, acted on, and applied **at the start of the next piece of work**, which means
this section has to reach back to
[section 4, phase 1](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd#phase-1-engagement-and-scoping).

The loop, in three steps:

1. **Record the lesson where the next analyst will look for it.** The analytical plan for the next
   cycle of a regular output, not a document nobody opens.
2. **Raise anything that applies beyond one output.** A method that did not work, a data quality
   problem, an assurance step that was disproportionate in either direction. The routes are in
   [section 13](../13-getting-help/index.qmd).
3. **Check the last cycle's lessons at scoping.** Phase 1 of the lifecycle asks what was learned last
   time. This is where the answer comes from.

Lessons that change how NHSBSA does analysis, rather than how one output is produced, go to the same
forum that runs the monthly cycle above, so that the guidance changes rather than the custom. It is
that forum rather than a new one, because a lesson and a guidance change are the same conversation
ten minutes apart, and a separate forum is a forum that will not meet.

## Public value

The Code's Value pillar asks three questions about a released output, and they are worth asking about
any analysis, not only official statistics.

- **Relevance to users.** Does it answer a question someone actually has? [Standard 8]
- **Clarity of presentation.** Can the intended reader understand it without help? [Standard 9]
- **Accessibility.** Can everyone who needs it get to it, including people using assistive
  technology? [Standard 10]

Standards 8, 9 and 10 bind official statistics. For everything else they are good practice, and they
are the cheapest quality improvement available, because an output nobody can use has no value however
well it was assured. See [section 9](../09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd) for what to do about the
answers.

## Recording a review

Keep the record proportionate. For most outputs the review is a short entry against the output in the
analytical plan: what was checked, what was found, what changed as a result, and who was involved.

For Business Critical analysis and for official statistics, the review is recorded formally and the
record is kept, because these are the outputs where someone will ask.

**Keep the record with the project record**, so that an output and everything said about it after
release sit in one place. A review filed separately from the analysis it reviews is a record nobody
finds when the analysis is next reused.
